| Templates | restored from a primary export via `qmrestore` (identical config on every node) | | |

Gaps: `scripts/verify-node.sh` checks ARC cap parity but does not check compression, ballooning drift, swap, or sysctl, so N2's 400 MB cap (a deliberate or stale local choice, `modprobe.d/zfs.conf`) was not flagged as "not canonical" beyond the ARC check, which only compares persisted vs live.

## 5. Detailed recommendations

All "how to measure" commands are read-only or tiny. All changes below are proposals; nothing was applied.

### P0-1. Fix memory pressure on N1/N4/N2 and add host reserve

What:
1. Immediate, live, reversible: `sysctl -w vm.swappiness=10` on N1, N2, N3, N4 (persist in `/etc/sysctl.d/99-nxeon-perf.conf`). Source: kernel docs `Documentation/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.rst` (swappiness); Proxmox admin guide warns about host swapping with ZFS ARC and VMs: https://pve.proxmox.com/wiki/Zfs_swap and "Memory Management" in https://pve.proxmox.com/pve-docs/pve-admin-guide.html#chapter_zfs.
2. Lower ARC where RAM is tight: N3 (32 GB RAM) `zfs_arc_max` 8 GB to 3-4 GB; N4 and N1 to 4 GB (the repo's own PRIMARY-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md already proposed this, but live nodes are still 8 GB). Live: `echo 4294967296 > /sys/module/zfs/parameters/zfs_arc_max`, persist in `/etc/modprobe.d/zfs-arc.conf` (+ `update-initramfs -u` on root-on-ZFS N2).
3. Re-balance: N5 has 21 GB free RAM and a 10 Gb link, N3 has about 3 GB, N2 13 GB. Target host reserve of at least 4-6 GB (plus ARC) so that sum(pinned VM RAM) <= RAM - ARC - 4 GB: N1 <= 52 GB, N4 <= 52 GB (today 66 and 77.8). Move or stop placing on N4; the scheduler's RAM guard (lib/node-ram-guard.ts) should be set to refuse N1/N4 for new RAM. Moves need a VM downtime window (non-clustered; the repo has a VM move engine).
4. N1 swap: see P2-2.

Benefit: eliminates swap-in latency (milliseconds per fault) for qemu pages and the OOM-kill class of failure that already took out the mail VM. Risk: swappiness=10 means the kernel will reclaim page cache earlier rather than swap; with the stale full swap it changes little immediately. Rollback: `sysctl -w vm.swappiness=60`. Measure: `vmstat 5` (si/so), `cat /proc/pressure/memory`, `grep -E 'SwapFree|MemAvailable' /proc/meminfo`, per-VM `VmSwap` from `/proc/<pid>/status`; journal `journalctl -k | grep -i oom`.

### P0-2. Remove leftover balloon floors (pin all customer VMs)

What: for each running customer VM with `balloon` < `memory`: `qm set <id> --balloon <memory>` (live; the repo documents this as live, no reboot, and notes that a monitor `balloon` command alone is undone by pvestatd). `scripts/pin-vm-memory.ts` already exists for this. Do it node by node AFTER P0-1 capacity is available (N1 would grow by 26 GB of commit: do not run on N1 until load is moved).

Benefit: honours paid RAM, ends the "1.82 GiB is not enough memory" class of game crash. Risk: host RAM demand rises by the "reclaimable" figures above (N1 +26 GB, N2 +20 GB, N3 +12 GB, N4 +6 GB, N5 +8 GB). N3 and N1 cannot absorb that today. Rollback: restore the old value. Measure: guest `free -m`, host `free -m`, `pvesh get /nodes/<n>/qemu/<id>/status/current` (`balloon`, `maxmem`).

Alternative honest option (owner decision): if capacity cannot be added, a smaller number of VMs per node is the only real fix; ballooning is a symptom.

### P0-3. N2 ARC cap

What: `echo 4294967296 > /sys/module/zfs/parameters/zfs_arc_max` (4 GB), then `echo 'options zfs zfs_arc_max=4294967296' > /etc/modprobe.d/zfs.conf` and `update-initramfs -u -k all` (root on ZFS: must be in the initramfs). 13.5 GB RAM is free today; N2 has 67.6 GB committed on 64 GB with ksmtuned merging; if P0-2 is applied on N2 the free RAM disappears, so 3-4 GB is the realistic ceiling there. Also decide on KSM: `ksmtuned` is active but `run=0`; KSM saves about 4.6 GB at the cost of CPU and is known to add latency jitter and a side-channel risk across tenants (Proxmox docs: https://pve.proxmox.com/wiki/Kernel_Samepage_Merging_(KSM)). Recommend leaving it off for game/latency-sensitive tenants, or keep as the emergency valve.

Benefit: ARC hit ratio rises, VM reads and clones are served from RAM (OpenZFS docs: https://openzfs.github.io/openzfs-docs/Performance%20and%20Tuning/Module%20Parameters.html#zfs-arc-max). Risk: low (live and reversible; ARC shrinks on demand). Canary: it is N2 alone. Measure: `awk '/^(hits|misses|size)/' /proc/spl/kstat/zfs/arcstats` before/after over the same hours; `arc_summary`; clone time of one template.

### P1-1. `iothread=1` and `ssd=1` on scsi0

What: set on template configs and provision: `qm set <tpl> --scsi0 vmdata:base-9000-disk-0,discard=on,iothread=1,ssd=1` (do for each template; templates are stopped, so the config is trivially changed; clones inherit it), and for existing VMs `qm set <id> --scsi0 <current volume>,discard=on,iothread=1,ssd=1` (takes effect on the next cold stop/start; PVE reports it as pending). `scsihw=virtio-scsi-single` is already right: each disk then gets its own controller and, with `iothread=1`, its own IO thread (Proxmox docs: https://pve.proxmox.com/wiki/Qemu/KVM_Virtual_Machines#qm_hard_disk, bus/controller and "IO Thread" paragraphs). `ssd=1` only exposes the non-rotational flag to the guest scheduler (harmless).

Do NOT add `cache=writeback` or `cache=unsafe`: they trade data safety for speed; `cache=none` (current default) with zvols is correct. Leave `aio` default (io_uring). No `iops/mbps` limits are set today, so one noisy VM can saturate a mirror: see section 7 for an optional safety valve.

Benefit: honest estimate, a modest reduction in IO latency and jitter under concurrent load; I did not benchmark (not allowed) so no number; published Proxmox forum and QEMU numbers show iothread gains mostly for multi-disk or high-IOPS workloads, minimal for single-disk idle ones. Risk: low; known historic problems (guest hang with iothread and old kernels) apply to very old guests (EL7); all templates are Debian 11+/Ubuntu 20.04+/Alma/Rocky 8+. Rollout: edit templates on N5 (lightest load), provision a canary VM, run a smoke test; then the other templates; existing VMs ride on the next customer reboot or a planned off-peak restart window (do not force restarts). Rollback: remove the options.

### P1-2. ZFS `compression=lz4` on the NVMe data pool (N1, N3, N4, N5)

What: `zfs set compression=lz4 data` (N1: `data/vms` inherits from `data`). Only newly written blocks are compressed; no downtime. lz4 is the OpenZFS default recommendation for general datasets and typically is net-positive or neutral for IO, as the CPU cost is tiny and it reduces writes (https://openzfs.github.io/openzfs-docs/Performance%20and%20Tuning/Workload%20Tuning.html). It also extends the life of the worn NVMes (P1-4). Caveat: VM disk images with already-compressed game data do not shrink; zero-filled or sparse regions do. Risk: very low; uses a little CPU on N1/N4 that already have CPU contention (N1 PSI 66 %: but lz4 costs well under 1 core at these write rates). Rollback: `zfs set compression=off data` (already-written blocks stay compressed, still readable). Measure: `zfs get compressratio`, `zpool iostat -v 5`, `zpool list` capacity.

Also set `atime=off` (or `relatime`) on the file datasets (`backup`, `tank/*`): zvols are unaffected; minor.

### P1-3. Virtio multiqueue

What: `qm set <id> --net0 virtio=<mac>,bridge=vmbr1,queues=<min(vcpus,4)>` plus in the guest the kernel auto-enables queues (`ethtool -L eth0 combined N` if needed). Proxmox docs: https://pve.proxmox.com/wiki/Qemu/KVM_Virtual_Machines#qm_network_device (Multiqueue). Benefit: parallel packet processing for busy game/web VMs and 4+ vCPU plans; none for 1 vCPU (leave `queues` off for 1-core plans). Needs a VM reboot. Honest note: current conntrack and NAT load are tiny (under 1000 entries, 29-62 rule lines) and no NIC drops are recorded on any node, so the NAT path is not the present bottleneck; low priority for customer traffic, but cheap for new provisions. Risk: low. Measure: guest `ethtool -S`, host `ip -s link` on the tap device (`tap<id>i0`) for drops, game tick/latency.

### P1-4. NVMe wear / hardware

N5 nvme (e8238fa6bf530001001b448b467a6c18): 80 % used, 271 TB written; N2 pair 54 % and 68 % used (109 TB each). On consumer-class drives, endurance exhaustion makes write latency erratic and a failed member degrades the mirror. Action (owner): order replacements before 90 %, schedule a mirror replace (`zpool replace`) in a maintenance window; compression (P1-2) and autotrim reduce write volume. Verify with `smartctl -a /dev/nvmeX` (read-only) monthly.

### P1-5. N1 CPU contention

N1: PSI `cpu some avg10=66 %`, 33 vCPUs on 8 threads, `%nice` 46 %. The source is test/agent runs (`tsx` workers at nice 19, `/tank/nxeon-wt-cfg-core`) running directly on the host with customer VMs (kodely-app, nexis-app, studionexis-soul, free VMs). Nice 19 helps but VMs are multi-thread qemu processes at default priority; the kernel CFS will still share. Move builds/tests to another box (the repo's own memory notes say dev apps were already moved to node-2; this is a recurrence) or put them in a cgroup with `CPUQuota`. Also N1 and N4 are 4.1:1 and 4.6:1 on 8 threads: consider a cap of about 3:1 for game VMs (game servers are single-thread-latency sensitive) and give heavy customers `cpuunits` (qm `--cpuunits` default 100; setting 200-400 on paying game servers and 50 on internal/dev VMs makes contention fall on the least important VMs). Measure with `/proc/pressure/cpu` and `perf sched` off-peak (read-only `cat` is enough).

### P2-1. autotrim

`zpool set autotrim=on data` (rpool on N2) or a monthly `zpool trim data` via cron/systemd (trim is IO-light but not free). Guests use `discard=on`, which frees zvol blocks, but with `autotrim=off` the NVMe controller is never told; sustained write performance is better when it knows free space. Docs: `man zpoolprops` (autotrim), https://openzfs.github.io/openzfs-docs/man/master/7/zpoolprops.7.html. On N1 `fstrim.timer` exists for the host root fs only. Risk: low-medium (TRIM load; some drives have slow TRIM); canary on N5 then N3. Measure: `zpool iostat -r`, `zpool status -t`.

### P2-2. N1 swap

N1 swap is an 8 GB zvol on the busiest VM pool, plus 2x1 GB NVMe partitions, all full. OpenZFS notes that swap on ZVOL can deadlock under heavy memory pressure (https://github.com/openzfs/zfs/issues/7734 and the Proxmox wiki https://pve.proxmox.com/wiki/Zfs_swap). Prefer a raw swap partition on NVMe, sized small (swap is a safety valve, not capacity). Do not remove swap without first fixing P0-1 or the next spike OOM-kills a VM. Needs a planned change; do on N1 only after load is moved.

### P2-3. Network sysctls (host)

Add to `/etc/sysctl.d/99-nxeon-perf.conf`: `net.core.default_qdisc=fq`, `net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr` (module `tcp_bbr`), `net.core.netdev_max_backlog=5000`, `net.core.rmem_max=16777216`, `net.core.wmem_max=16777216`, `net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0`. Benefit applies to host-originated and forwarded TCP only if the guests inherit it (guests have their own stack: BBR on the HOST only affects host sockets, not guest TCP). Honest: for NAT-forwarded guest traffic the host's congestion control does not apply, and game servers are mostly UDP, so the real benefit is limited to host services (backups, API). Low priority. Roll out with `sysctl -w`, rollback by deleting the file. Source: https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/ip-sysctl.html.

### P2-4. Ring buffers and offloads

N1/N2/N4 igb/e1000e have RX/TX rings at 256 (hardware max 4096). `ethtool -G <if> rx 1024 tx 1024` (live, brief link blip). No RX drops are recorded now (N4 shows `missed 132` in 2 weeks, negligible), so benefit is unproven; do it only if monitoring shows bursts. N2's e1000e has TSO off: this is a known workaround for the e1000e "Detected Hardware Unit Hang" bug; leave it unless the cause is confirmed.

### P3 Not recommended / low value (and why)

- `mitigations=off`: on i7-7700K Kaby Lake the retbleed/IBRS and MDS mitigations cost real performance, but this is a multi-tenant host with customer VMs and `vmscape`/L1TF/MDS apply; turning them off exposes tenants to each other and the host. Not recommended. The kernel already uses `IBRS` for retbleed, which is the costly variant on this CPU generation; hardware upgrade to a newer generation is the clean fix. SMT stays on (security vs capacity: turning SMT off halves vCPUs).
- Hugepages (HugeTLB) for VMs: THP is already giving qemu 8-11 GB of transparent huge pages (AnonHugePages). Static hugepages would remove the ability to balloon/overcommit and need a reboot; not worth it.
- NUMA / CPU pinning: all hosts are single-NUMA; pinning makes oversubscription worse.
- `cache=writeback/unsafe`, `nobarrier`, `sync=disabled`: data-loss risk; do not.
- Switching `cpu: host` to a baseline model: would reduce performance.
- q35 machine type: no gain for virtio guests.
- ZFS special/log/cache devices: there are no spare devices (2 NVMe + 1 HDD per node); L2ARC would cost ARC RAM, which is scarce. A SLOG is useless since `sync=standard` zvols with cache=none guests mostly do async writes.

---

## 6. How to measure before/after without hurting customers

All of this is read-only and cheap; do it at the same hours on consecutive days (customer load varies). Peak-hour numbers do not exist yet: set up collection first.

1. Start a 24-48 h baseline: run `sar`/sysstat (installed on N1/N2 only; install `sysstat` on N3/N4/N5, which is a small package change) or simply log every 60 s to a file: `/proc/pressure/{cpu,memory,io}`, `vmstat 1 2`, `/proc/spl/kstat/zfs/arcstats` (hits/misses/size), `zpool iostat -v 1 2`, `/proc/meminfo` (MemAvailable, SwapFree), `ip -s link` on uplink + `tap*`. PSI (`avg10/avg60/avg300`) is the single best "is it slow" metric: it measures real stall time, not utilisation.
2. Guest-level latency without load: from a canary VM, `ping`/`mtr` to the node gateway (read only); game-level: server tick time from the game's own console (Minecraft `/tps`, Valheim/Terraria logs); a tiny `fio` is NOT allowed per rules, so use `iostat -x 5` (host: `iostat -x 5 nvme0n1 nvme1n1`: `r_await`, `w_await`, `aqu-sz`, `%util`) and `zpool iostat -l` (latency columns: `total_wait`, `disk_wait`, `syncq_wait`, `asyncq_wait`) as the IO latency before/after.
3. Per-change metric: P0-1 swap-in/out rate + `memory some` PSI + OOM count; P0-3 ARC hit ratio + clone time; P1-1 `zpool iostat -l` write/read wait and guest `iostat -x`; P1-2 `compressratio` + device write bytes (`smartctl` Data Units Written delta per day); P1-3 tap drops + guest softirq; P1-5 CPU PSI.
4. Do canary then fleet: N5 (low load, 10 Gb) first, then N3 (low CPU PSI), then N2, then N4, then N1 last (busiest and most fragile). Off-peak windows: node-local night (SGP 02:00-06:00 local = 18:00-22:00 UTC; FSN 03:00-05:00 CET; BHS 03:00-05:00 EST); I do not have actual customer traffic curves, so use the sar/PSI baseline to choose.

---

## 7. Other findings and open questions (honest uncertainty)

- **No per-VM IO or CPU limits**: with a mirror of consumer-class NVMe and 17 VMs on N4, a single VM doing a world save/backup/`apt upgrade` can raise latency for all. An optional safety valve is `mbps_rd/mbps_wr` bursts or `iops_rd/wr` caps on the scsi disk (a high cap that only trips abusers, e.g. 4000 IOPS / 200 MB/s with `iops_max` burst). Needs a reboot; I have NOT validated sensible numbers (no benchmarks allowed). Treat as optional.
- **Pool fullness**: N1 `data` 68 % full with 70 % fragmentation, N4 `data` 65 % full: ZFS write performance degrades from about 80 % and with high fragmentation. N1/N4 are at the edge for 16 K random-write VM workloads. Free space or add capacity before 80 %; `refreservation=none` plus sparse zvols mean "free" is overcommitted (sum of volsizes vs pool size should be checked: N1 provisioned zvols are about 700 GB nominal on a 358 GB pool; thin provisioning risk of pool-full stalls).
- **HDD backup pools** are single-disk, no redundancy, and ashift is `0` (auto) on N1 `tank`: the actual vdev ashift was not read (`zdb -C` would show it); if it is 9 on a 4K drive writes are amplified. Backup-only, low priority.
- **Linked-clone provisioning** exists only for the golden game template and is gated by env flags; its effect on steady-state IO is expected to be neutral but I could not verify the live env flags from here (the worker environment was not read).
- **N2 kernel/PVE are older** than the other nodes (7.0.2-6 / 9.2.2 vs 7.0.14-x / 9.2.18-20): same-major, but consider bringing them in line during a reboot window (reboot required; kernel updates also reset the hardware counters and run all VMs through downtime).
- **No real steal figure**: nodes are bare metal, so "steal" is the guest's view only (the host /proc/stat guest column `gu`=0 was shown); guest-side `%st` must be read inside VMs (not done: customer VMs untouched). CPU PSI on the host is the proxy used.
- **KSM + THP** interplay on N2: KSM only merges when `run=1`; it is currently 0, so the 4.6 GB "saved" is a stale count. If `ksmtuned` flips `run=1` under pressure, expect CPU spikes and some latency jitter. Unverified: whether anything on N2 turns it on.
- **Data freshness**: all numbers are one snapshot from 2026-10-02 17:46-17:50 UTC (afternoon in Europe, middle of the night in Singapore), so N2/N5 load looks low and N4/N1 high at this moment; CPU PSI at peak is unknown.
- The N4 balloon per-VM live loop in my probe stopped early (4 of 17 shown), so live balloon values for N4 come from `qm config` only; they were consistent with 14 of 17 pinned.

## 8. Quick wins that need NO reboot (all live, reversible)

1. `sysctl -w vm.swappiness=10` on N1-N4 (and persist in a sysctl.d file).
2. N2: raise `zfs_arc_max` to 3-4 GB live. N3/N4/N1: lower to 3-4 GB live if memory pressure persists.
3. `zfs set compression=lz4 data` on N1, N3, N4, N5.
4. `qm set <id> --balloon <memory>` for the 30 VMs still floor-limited, node by node, only where the node has headroom (N5 and N2 first; N1/N3 after capacity is added).
5. `zpool set autotrim=on` (canary N5), or monthly `zpool trim`.
6. Move agent/test jobs off N1 (or cap them with a systemd `CPUQuota`).
7. Optional: `ethtool -G` rings, BBR/fq sysctls (small value).

Apply to NEW provisions only (no customer impact): `iothread=1,ssd=1` on template scsi0 for templates 9000-9009 and 9101 on each node; `queues=` in provision net0; keep `balloon=memory` (already default). Apply to EXISTING VMs with a customer reboot: `iothread`, `ssd`, `queues`.

The report is written to /root/research/perf-hypervisor.md. It has a prioritised summary table first, then per-node facts, VM conformity, a repo-versus-Proxmox-defaults comparison, detailed recommendations with sources, a measurement plan and a no-reboot quick-wins list. Everything was read-only. I changed nothing on the nodes and printed no secrets. The raw captures are in the scratchpad `h/` folder under /tmp/claude-0/-root/4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc/scratchpad/.

All numbers come from one snapshot at 17:46-17:50 UTC, so peak-hour behaviour is not measured. The report says so. I did not run benchmarks, so none of the expected benefits has a measured number behind it.

**What is already fine**
- All 56 running VMs and all templates use `cpu: host`, virtio-scsi-single, virtio net and the guest agent.
- Governors are `performance` everywhere, every host has a single NUMA node, and all pools are NVMe mirrors with ashift 12.
- Conntrack and NAT load are tiny. Conntrack is at most 909 of 262,144 entries, and there are no NIC drops.
- Config is identical across nodes. There is no old-versus-new VM drift except ballooning.

**Main findings**
1. **Memory is the biggest problem, on the primary (N1) and N4.**
   - N1 swap is 10.2 of 10.2 GB used. The host OOM-killed VM 8000 (nxeon-mail) on 2026-09-25 at 12:02.
   - N4 swap is 2.0 of 2.0 GB, with 2 GB free RAM, and ZFS ARC is starved (`arc_no_grow=1`).
   - Configured VM RAM exceeds host RAM on N1 (66 GB on 64), N2 (67.6 on 64) and N4 (77.8 on 64). N4's balloon floors alone are 67.6 GB.
   - The repo's pin policy only applies at provision and resize time. 30 of 56 running VMs still have the old 50% balloon floor, about 73 GB reclaimable. That covers N1 (11 of 13 VMs), N3 (5 of 6) and N5 (5 of 8), plus N2 and N4.
   - Pinning the rest needs capacity moved first. N5 has 21 GB free.
2. **N2's ZFS ARC is capped at 400 MB.** It is set in `/etc/modprobe.d/zfs.conf` and ignores the onboarding script's 8 GB default. The node has 13.5 GB free RAM and its ARC hit ratio is 87% (others about 91-95%). This probably explains the 67.7 s full clone measured on 2026-10-01. N3's ARC is 8 GB on a 32 GB node.
3. **Disks:** no VM has `iothread=1` (or `ssd=1`), even though the controller is virtio-scsi-single. The platform never sets disk options at create time; they come from the templates.
4. **ZFS:** `compression=off` on the VM pools of N1, N3, N4 and N5 (N2 compresses), and `autotrim=off` everywhere. N1 is 68% full with 70% fragmentation, and N4 is 65% full.
5. **N1 CPU:**
   - CPU pressure is 66% over the last 10 seconds, with 33 vCPUs on 8 threads.
   - Most of it is niced `tsx` test/agent jobs from `/tank/nxeon-wt-cfg-core` running on the host.
6. **NVMe wear:** N5 has one drive at 80% used (271 TB written) and N2's pair are at 54% and 68%.
7. **Smaller items:**
   - KSM merged about 4.6 GB on N2 and is stale (`run=0`).
   - N2 runs an older kernel and PVE than the other nodes.
   - N2's e1000e has TSO off.
   - There are no per-VM IO or CPU limits, and no `queues=` on net.
   - Only `ip_forward` is set as a host sysctl.

**Order of changes in the report**
- **No-reboot quick wins:**
  - `vm.swappiness=10`, plus ARC cap changes (raise N2 to 3-4 GB, lower N3/N4/N1 to 3-4 GB).
  - `zfs set compression=lz4`, autotrim canaried on N5, and moving the test jobs off N1.
  - Pinning balloons, node by node, only where there is headroom.
- **Needs a VM cold restart or new provisions only:** `iothread=1,ssd=1` on the templates and on existing VMs, and `queues=` for 2+ vCPU VMs.
- **Not recommended, with reasons:** `mitigations=off`, static hugepages, CPU pinning, `cache=writeback`, `sync=disabled`, L2ARC/SLOG, and a q35 machine type.

Each item in the report includes risk, canary order (N5, then N3, N2, N4, N1 last), rollback, and read-only measurement metrics such as CPU/memory/IO pressure stall info, `zpool iostat -l` and ARC stats.

**Unverified:** the live env flags for the linked-clone provisioning, the actual vdev ashift of N1's backup HDD pool, whether anything turns KSM on at N2, and guest-side steal. N4's per-VM live balloon loop stopped early, so its balloon figures come from `qm config` only.

**Main findings**
- **Memory pressure on the primary and node-4.**
  - The primary's swap is full (10.2 of 10.2 GB), and the host OOM-killed the mail VM (8000) on 2026-09-25.
  - Node-4's swap is full, with 2 GB RAM free.
  - VM RAM is overcommitted on the primary (66 GB on a 64 GB host), node-2 (67.6 GB on 64) and node-4 (77.8 GB on 64).
- **Leftover balloon floors.** 30 of 56 running VMs still have the old 50% floor, about 73 GB reclaimable. The repo's pin policy only applies to new provisions and resizes. Pinning the rest needs capacity moved first; node-5 has about 21 GB free.

**Suggested order**
- **No reboot:**
  - Lower `vm.swappiness` to 10 and adjust the ARC caps (raise node-2's, lower node-3's and node-4's).
  - Turn on `compression=lz4` and pin balloons where a node has headroom.
  - Move the test jobs off the primary.
- **Needs a customer reboot, or new provisions only:** `iothread` and `ssd` on the disks, and multiqueue on net for VMs with 2 or more vCPUs.
